title: Rub the rim of a water-filled singing bowl and it flings off droplets

cover.alt: A brass Tibetan singing bowl full of water, its surface white with ripples and tiny droplets.

body: A Tibetan singing bowl is played by striking or rubbing its rim with a wooden or leather-wrapped mallet, which sets its metal walls vibrating, much like a wet finger circling a wine glass. Fill the bowl with water and the shaking walls make waves on the surface, starting at the edge. Rub harder and the waves grow and turn chaotic until the surface breaks up, throwing droplets into the air. Physicists Denis Terwagne and John Bush studied the effect in 2011, driving bowls with sound so they could turn the shaking up step by step.

slides.alt: A dark mallet circles the rim of a brass bowl full of water. Ripples spread across the water, and the surface turns frothy and glittering with droplets.
slides.caption: A mallet circles the rim of a water-filled singing bowl. As the bowl vibrates, ripples cover the water, then the surface glitters with flying droplets.

slides.heading: Faraday got there first
slides.text: In 1831 Michael Faraday found that a layer of liquid shaken up and down stays flat until the shaking passes a critical strength. Then it breaks into standing waves that bob at half the shaking frequency. In a singing bowl, the shaking comes from the walls, so the waves start at the edge.

slides.question: Why are singing bowls especially good at making these waves?
options: They vibrate at a fairly low frequency
slides.explanation: Terwagne and Bush concluded that the bowl's relatively low vibration frequency makes it an efficient generator of waves driven from the edge.
